title: WebSockets
short: Keep a line open so the server can push news the moment it happens.
what: Normal HTTP is ask, then answer: the server can't speak first. A WebSocket starts as one HTTP request, then stays open as a two-way line. Either side can send a message at any time, so chat messages and live scores arrive at once.
analogy: Keeping a phone call open, instead of texting 'anything new?' every 5 seconds.

frames.say: Alice and Bob chat through a server. When Bob sends a message, Alice's screen should show it right away.
With plain HTTP the server can't speak first, so Alice's app asks every 5 seconds: 12 requests a minute, most answered 'no'.
WebSocket: Alice sends one HTTP request asking to upgrade. The server answers 101 Switching Protocols and keeps the line open.
Bob's app does the same. The server now holds one open connection per online user, and either side can send at any time.
Bob sends 'hi Alice!' on his connection. Each message costs a few bytes of framing, not hundreds of bytes of HTTP headers.
The server pushes it down Alice's open connection at once. No asking, and no waiting up to 5 seconds for the next poll.
With millions online, Alice and Bob sit on different servers. A pub/sub channel carries Bob's message to the server holding Alice's line.

when: The server must push updates the moment they happen
Polling would mostly come back with 'nothing new'
python:
import math

bob_sends_at = [13, 31, 47]          # seconds into the minute

# Polling: Alice's app asks "anything new?" every 5 seconds
asks = 60 // 5
waits = [math.ceil(t / 5) * 5 - t for t in bob_sends_at]
print("polling:", asks, "requests,", asks - len(bob_sends_at), "empty")
print("polling waits:", waits, "seconds")

# WebSocket: one handshake, then the server pushes each message
print("websocket: 1 handshake,", len(bob_sends_at), "pushes, waits 0 seconds")
output:
polling: 12 requests, 9 empty
polling waits: [2, 4, 3] seconds
websocket: 1 handshake, 3 pushes, waits 0 seconds
watch: Connections drop when phones switch networks: reconnect, then fetch what you missed.
Each open connection pins a server. The load balancer must allow long-lived connections.
For one-way updates (server to client), server-sent events or long polling may be enough.
interview: Design WhatsApp or a chat app
